strengths: The task is well motivated: combining a reference photograph with a description of appearance changes addresses a useful gap between person re-identification and composed image retrieval. SynCPR and the manually annotated ITCPR benchmark could provide valuable resources for this research community.

The experiments provide substantial evidence that SynCPR is useful. In Table 1, training on SynCPR increases CaLa's Rank-1 accuracy from 24.02% to 39.33% and SPRC's from 25.07% to 42.27%, demonstrating benefits beyond the proposed model.

FAFA improves over the strongest comparison trained on the same data: 46.54% versus 42.27% Rank-1 and 55.60% versus 51.62% mAP. Table 2 supports the contribution of FDA, while the additional CIRR results provide encouraging evidence of applicability beyond the authors' benchmark.

The presentation is generally understandable, with useful pipeline diagrams, explicit objectives, extensive generation prompts, and substantial implementation details in the appendix. Manually reviewing additional gallery candidates to correct false negatives is a worthwhile benchmark construction step.
weaknesses: The principal concern is evaluation independence. Appendix B.1.3 describes ITCPR as exclusively a test set, yet Section 4.3 and Figure S13 select the soft-label strength, feature count, filtering threshold, auxiliary-loss weights, and masking ratio using retrieval performance on this benchmark. No separate validation protocol is documented. An untouched test evaluation is needed to establish that the reported gains survive this extensive model and data selection.

The central claims of high-quality, identity-consistent synthetic data are insufficiently quantified. Selected examples and one MLLM's scores do not establish the retained dataset's identity error rate, caption accuracy, or demographic coverage. There is no independent human audit or scorer calibration, and the benefits of paired generation, LoRA adaptation, and varying LoRA strength are not isolated through controlled downstream ablations. The filtering experiment also changes dataset size alongside quality.

The modality comparisons do not fully establish the necessity of the proposed composition mechanism. Image-only, text-only, and late-fusion baselines use different training data from FAFA. Although the same-data CIR comparisons are valuable, matched-backbone unimodal and late-fusion models trained on SynCPR are needed to separate composition benefits from training-data advantages. Results by source dataset and extent of clothing change would also clarify what ITCPR measures.

Important reproducibility details remain unspecified, including the reconstruction decoder architecture, feature dimensions and query count, the epsilon used in Equation 4, and minibatch construction for obtaining same-GID partial positives. No repeated-run uncertainty is reported. This particularly limits confidence in the smaller auxiliary-loss gains: adding MFR to FDA plus FD yields only 0.49 percentage points in Rank-1 and 0.11 in mAP.

The originality is primarily in the person-specific data construction and integration. FAFA builds on BLIP-2 with top-k similarity aggregation, diversity regularization, and feature reconstruction. The relationship to existing CIR data construction and synthetic-triplet approaches, including cited work such as CASE and CompoDiff, needs clearer discussion to substantiate the broader novelty claims.

The privacy motivation needs a more complete treatment of the actual data sources and application. The generator is adapted using real person images, and ITCPR uses identifiable people from existing datasets, but applicable licenses, consent provenance, and redistribution conditions are not discussed. Demographic bias and misuse considerations for person retrieval are also absent. Synthetic training triplets alone do not resolve these issues.
